In particular, some experts argued that they do not believe existing risk management activities and policy efforts adequately consider the potential risk of humans losing control over hypothetical future misaligned artificial general intelligence (AGI) systems (Bengio, 2024[257]; Cass-Beggs, 2024[293]; Faggella, 2024[294]; Taylor, 2023[295]),4 which they see as an extreme potential outcome of insufficient AI safety measures, especially those for AI alignment.

They argue that, regardless of testing, developers and deployers of some types of advanced AI systems have such a limited understanding of their system’s capabilities or how they may react to novel scenarios that they cannot guarantee their safety. This “loss of control” is a subject of disagreement among Expert Group members and the broader AI community.

Consider AGI with advanced computer programming abilities able to break out of the box and engage with the world across cyberspace, thanks to a designed-in internet connection or use of side-channel attacks. It could possess agency beyond human control, operate autonomously, and make decisions with far-reaching consequences.
In the extreme, a loss-of-control scenario could result, wherein AGI's pursuit of its desired objectives incentivizes the machine to resist being turned off, counter to human efforts.
U.S. policy also encourages the safe development of frontier AI models to avoid catastrophic consequences of AGI misuse, misalignment, or loss of control.

As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become increasingly capable and diffused throughout the economy and society, the possibility of loss of control (LOC) incidents in which AI systems operate outside human control may require new national-level responses. In this paper, the authors describe the case for a national plan to respond to LOC incidents and propose key criteria and an outline to get started.

As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become increasingly capable and diffused throughout the economy and society, the possibility of loss of control (LOC) incidents—in which AI systems operate outside meaningful human control—may require new national response capabilities, preparedness, and planning.

quote: Experiments in controlled conditions increasingly find that advanced AI models demonstrate behavior that could evade human control, including deceiving or blackmailing users to prevent themselves from being replaced or shut down. Although these real-world incidents and experimental findings may be detected and quickly remediated, there is potential for LOC incidents to escalate to greater levels of harm, particularly if they occur in high-stakes domains or if human oversight is too slow or insufficient before serious consequences unfold.

quote: We define LOC incidents as incidents in which AI systems operate outside meaningful human control.

We define rogue AI as an AI system that is responsible for LOC incidents regardless of whether the LOC was accidental or resulted from external manipulation. In other words, our definition encompasses scenarios in which humans have inadvertently deployed an AI system without adequate control mechanisms, humans deliberately create or deploy rogue AI systems for malicious purposes, and advanced AI systems themselves develop capabilities that enable them to evade human control.

Our definition can be compared with the definition of LOC scenario from the 2025 United Kingdom (UK) AI Safety Report, which reads: 'Loss of control scenario: A scenario in which one or more general-purpose AI systems come to operate outside of anyone's control, with no clear path to regaining control' (AI Safety Institute, International AI Safety Report 2025, Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, UK Government, February 18, 2025) (emphasis added).
